strengths: Broad empirical scope: the paper validates ConDA on five genuinely diverse spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, two-photon calcium imaging, TMS-induced E-fields, facial action units, and monkey motor cortex spiking), which is an ambitious and useful demonstration of generality.

The dual-space design (lossy, compact contrastive embedding C for editing vs. near-lossless diffusion latent Z for rendering) is a clean and sensible architectural idea that cleanly separates concerns of controllability and fidelity.

Reasonably thorough ablations are included: embedding dimensionality sweep (Fig. 13), comparison against PCA and beta-VAE baselines (Table 2), comparison against CcGAN as an alternative generator backbone (Appendix C.2), and an orthogonality/disentanglement probe (Table 6).

Good engineering/reproducibility documentation in the appendix (detailed simulation protocols for fluid and TMS data, training hyperparameters, parameter counts, and runtime tables), and a promise to open-source code and the fluid benchmark dataset.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core pipeline largely stitches together existing components (DDIM inversion, the CEBRA supervised contrastive encoder from prior work, kNN neighborhood lifting, and standard spline/Taylor/LSTM traversal operators). The paper's own related-work section acknowledges contrastive-learning identifiability results exist, but ConDA provides no new theoretical guarantee or analysis of why/when this composition yields identifiable or dynamics-aligned structure beyond empirical demonstration.

Potential evaluation artifact in Table 1: the near-zero RMSE reported for the Spline method (and very low RMSE for TEX-2) in C-space raises concern about whether the spline is fit to the same points at which it is subsequently evaluated (near-interpolation), which would trivially yield near-zero error regardless of the quality of the underlying representation; the paper does not clarify the train/held-out protocol for this specific metric, undermining confidence in the headline quantitative claims.

The comparison in Fig. 5/Table (monkey reach data) between ConDA (a supervised method using velocity/reach labels) and PCA (a fully unsupervised method) is not apples-to-apples; the improvement could stem largely from the use of label supervision rather than from any specific benefit of contrastive structuring. A supervised linear or regression baseline using the same labels would be a fairer comparison.

Some clinical/scientific claims are overreached relative to the evidence: the TMS responder-classification results are modest (e.g., F1=0.63, small and imbalanced sample of 110 patients, 30 responders vs. 80 non-responders) yet are used to motivate strong claims about a 'tangible path to personalized targeting,' which is not well supported by such modest classification performance.

Reproducibility is uneven across domains: code and the fluid dataset are promised to be released, but the calcium imaging data requires author permission and the TMS patient MRI/HAMD data cannot be released at all (HIPAA), meaning full reproduction of 2 of 5 core experiments is not possible for external reviewers/readers.

The paper's disentanglement/orthogonality evidence (Table 6) is reported for only one dataset (fluid, time vs. Reynolds number) despite the broader claim that latent traversal directions reflect underlying dynamical factors across all five domains; this leaves the generality of the disentanglement claim largely unverified.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy in Section 3, with many overloaded symbols (Z, C, T_eta, h_psi, l, f_theta) introduced in quick succession, which reduces accessibility; some figures (e.g., Fig. 1, Fig. 2) are visually cluttered and would benefit from clearer captions tied directly to the metrics reported in the tables.

strengths: Evaluates across an unusually broad range of five spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, calcium imaging, facial expression, TMS/E-field neurostimulation, and monkey motor cortex), which is ambitious in scope.

The overall architectural idea of separating a lossy, dynamics-aligned compact embedding (for editing) from a near-lossless diffusion feature space (for rendering) is a sensible engineering principle.
Reasonably thorough appendix with implementation details (training iterations, optimizer settings, dataset acquisition pipelines) that aids reproducibility in principle.
Includes several baselines (Lerp, Slerp, LSTM, TEX-1, PCA, beta-VAE, CcGAN) spanning linear and nonlinear approaches, which at least attempts a fair comparison landscape.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is limited: the method is largely a combination of pre-existing components (off-the-shelf CEBRA contrastive embeddings, standard DDIM inversion, kNN-based latent lifting, and classical spline/Taylor extrapolation), with no new theoretical contribution, identifiability guarantee, or genuinely new algorithmic mechanism beyond assembling known pieces.

Several key quantitative results look implausibly strong (e.g., RMSE of exactly 0.00 for Spline/TEX-2 in C-space across multiple datasets in Table 1), suggesting the trajectory-fitting evaluation may not be done on held-out points distinct from those used to fit the spline/Taylor expansion -- this raises serious concerns about evaluation methodology and potential leakage that the paper does not clarify or rule out.

The kNN 'lifting' decoder requires storing and querying the entire training set of (c, z) pairs, which is effectively a memorization/retrieval mechanism rather than a generative model; this undermines claims of 'generation' and could trivially inflate fidelity metrics by retrieving near-identical stored training latents rather than truly extrapolating/interpolating dynamics.

Downstream classification results that are central to the clinical motivation (responder vs. non-responder TMS E-field classification) remain weak in absolute terms (F1 ~0.62-0.66, AUC ~0.67-0.68), which is far from convincing evidence of practical clinical utility despite the paper's optimistic framing ('a tangible and interpretable path toward personalizing targeting strategies').

Evidence for 'disentanglement'/interpretability rests on a single, narrow metric (cosine similarity between two linear regression coefficient vectors on one dataset, Table 6) rather than a systematic disentanglement study (e.g., multiple factors, multiple datasets, established disentanglement metrics such as MIG or DCI).

The ablation against PCA and beta-VAE (Table 2) conflates representation learning and decoder architecture differences, making it hard to isolate whether gains stem from the contrastive objective itself versus other pipeline differences (e.g., kNN lifting vs. learned decoders for baselines).

Internal inconsistency suggests insufficient polish: the appendix title ('Nonlinearly Controllable Counterfactuals with Diffusion') does not match the main paper title ('Contrastive Diffusion Alignment'), indicating the submission may be a patchwork of an earlier draft rather than a fully coherent, carefully finalized manuscript.

The method fundamentally requires labeled/conditioned auxiliary variables y for every sample to build contrastive positive/negative pairs, which is a significant practical limitation not adequately foregrounded as a core constraint (most 'controllable generation' settings of interest may lack dense auxiliary labels).

Limitations section is extremely brief (a single sentence) and does not seriously engage with the issues above (potential leakage, retrieval-based decoding, label dependency, generalization beyond training-adjacent trajectories).
Some reported real-world, sensitive clinical data (HAMD scores, patient E-fields) cannot be released, limiting reproducibility of the most application-relevant results, though this is disclosed.

strengths: Impressive breadth of empirical validation across five genuinely different spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, calcium imaging, TMS E-fields, facial expression AUs, and monkey reach spiking), which is unusual and valuable for demonstrating generality of a representation-learning idea.

The dual-space design (lossy, dynamics-aligned compact embedding C for editing vs. near-lossless feature latent Z for rendering) is a clean, well-motivated architectural idea that cleanly separates concerns of controllability and fidelity.

Reasonably thorough ablations: comparisons against PCA, β-VAE, Lerp/Slerp, LSTM, and first- vs second-order Taylor expansion, as well as an orthogonality/disentanglement analysis (Table 6) and an embedding-dimensionality sweep (Fig. 13).

Strong effort on reproducibility: extensive appendix detailing simulation pipelines (FEniCS Navier-Stokes, SimNIBS E-field modeling), hyperparameters, algorithmic pseudocode (Stages A-C), and compute/runtime tables.

The therapeutic neurostimulation use case (KDE-based responder/non-responder class interpolation) is a compelling, clinically motivated application that illustrates potential downstream utility beyond toy benchmarks.
weaknesses: Several reported results raise concerns about evaluation rigor rather than genuine generalization: Table 1 shows Spline achieving RMSE = 0.00 on multiple datasets, which is suspicious and suggests the spline may be evaluated on (or fit directly through) the same points used for 'reconstruction,' rather than on a genuinely held-out test trajectory; this needs much clearer clarification of train/validation/test protocol for trajectory metrics.

The core technical contribution is largely a composition of existing, well-known components (CEBRA/InfoNCE contrastive embedding, splines, finite-difference Taylor expansion, kNN regression, DDIM inversion) applied to diffusion latents; the paper does not clearly establish new theoretical understanding (e.g., identifiability guarantees for the embedding) beyond empirical performance gains, despite related work claiming 'identifiability' as a gap it fills.

No direct quantitative comparison against the conditioning-based baselines explicitly criticized in the introduction (ControlNet, InstructPix2Pix) or against recent geometry-preserving diffusion traversal methods (Wang & Golland 2023; Hahm et al. 2024) that are cited as closely related; comparisons are limited to simple Lerp/Slerp/LSTM, which weakens the claim of 'improved controllability compared to...conditioning-based baselines.'

The supervised contrastive objective requires auxiliary condition/time labels for every training pair; the paper does not discuss sensitivity to label noise/sparsity or scenarios where such dense condition labels are unavailable, limiting the generality claimed in the abstract.

Evaluation metrics (PSNR/SSIM/RMSE) are reported with modest sample sizes and no statistical significance testing; some improvements (e.g., C vs Z for Lerp/Slerp baselines) are marginal and may not be meaningful given reported standard deviations.

The kNN-based lifting from C back to Z inherently limits extrapolation to regions near training data manifolds, yet the paper claims faithful 'extrapolation' capability without clearly testing extrapolation beyond the training distribution's support.

Presentation issues: the appendix title ('Nonlinearly Controllable Counterfactuals with Diffusion') does not match the main paper title, suggesting incomplete editing/rebranding; some notation is overloaded (e.g., reuse of hat notation for different edited quantities), reducing clarity.

Limitations section is very brief (three bullet-style phrases) and does not substantively discuss the leakage/evaluation concerns, scalability to larger/more complex videos, or computational cost trade-offs of the added contrastive-training and kNN-lifting stages.

strengths: Broad empirical validation across five genuinely diverse spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, calcium imaging, TMS-induced E-fields, facial expressions, and monkey motor cortex spiking), which is unusual breadth for a single paper and lends some credibility to the claim of generality.

Reasonably thorough set of ablations: solver-agnosticism (DDIM vs. Rex-RK4, cLDM vs. IsoDiff), kNN vs. MLP lifting decoder, embedding dimensionality sweep (Fig. 10), and comparison against PCA/beta-VAE baselines.

The conceptual separation of 'editing' (in a compact contrastive space) from 'rendering' (in the original diffusion latent space) is a clean and intuitively appealing design, and the algorithmic pipeline (Algorithms 1-2) is spelled out in enough detail to aid reproducibility.

Appendices provide substantial detail on dataset acquisition/simulation (FEM fluid sim, SimNIBS E-field pipeline, DISFA, calcium imaging, MC_Maze), which supports reproducibility for domain-specific parts of the work.
Applications to biomedical/scientific domains (TMS responder/non-responder class transfer, monkey reach kinematics) suggest plausible downstream utility beyond generic image editing.
weaknesses: The PDF itself contains a visibly broken/leftover section (page 8, 'D REVISED RESULTS' with orphaned LaTeX line numbers 1415-1457 and a truncated table) that appears to be an artifact of careless merging/editing. This is a serious presentation defect that raises doubts about how carefully the rest of the submission (and its reported numbers) were checked.

The core technical contribution largely amounts to applying an existing off-the-shelf contrastive method (CEBRA, Schneider et al. 2023) on top of pretrained diffusion latents, combined with standard interpolation/extrapolation tools (cubic splines, finite-difference Taylor expansion, LSTM) and a kNN decoder. Little of this is newly proposed; the novelty is primarily in the systems-level combination and application to diffusion latents rather than in new modeling or theoretical contributions.

Near-zero RMSE values reported for Spline/TEX-2 in C-space (e.g., 0.00 in several rows of Table 1) are suspicious and under-explained: if the spline is fit directly to the full observed embedding sequence and then evaluated at the same points used for fitting (as the interpolation task description suggests: 'we regenerate intermediate frames under observed conditions'), this risks a circular/self-fulfilling comparison rather than a genuine held-out interpolation test. The paper does not clearly clarify whether fitted points are excluded from evaluation.

Despite extensive framing in the introduction and related work around ControlNet, InstructPix2Pix, and NoiseCLR as inadequate baselines, no quantitative head-to-head comparison against these conditioning-based methods is actually presented in the experiments; comparisons are limited to Lerp/Slerp/LSTM/PCA/beta-VAE, which are comparatively weak baselines and may overstate the method's advantage.

Central claims about improved 'interpretability' rest mostly on qualitative visualizations (Fig. 3, Fig. 5) and a single cosine-similarity orthogonality metric (Table 12) rather than systematic quantitative or human-subject evaluation of interpretability, making this core claim less rigorously supported than the fidelity/PSNR claims.

CEBRA-based embedding learning requires per-frame auxiliary labels for every dataset, which is a substantive practical limitation not clearly foregrounded as a core requirement/limitation of the framework (rather than a minor implementation detail), potentially restricting applicability to settings lacking dense auxiliary annotations.

The abstract and results section highlight cherry-picked headline numbers (e.g., '35.7 PSNR vs. 28.3 for linear baselines') without similarly foregrounding weaker results (e.g., calcium imaging RMSE that is often higher, not lower, for Lerp/Slerp vs. ConDA C-space per Table 1, e.g., Ca2+ Lerp RMSE 43.87 in C-space vs. 16.60 in Z-space, an apparent regression that is not discussed).

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important and underexplored problem: giving diffusion latent spaces an explicit, controllable geometry tied to auxiliary variables such as time or stimulation parameters.

The empirical scope is broad, spanning five very different spatiotemporal domains (fluid simulation, calcium imaging, TMS E-fields, facial action units, and monkey motor cortex spiking), which is an ambitious attempt at generality.

The paper includes a large number of ablations (solver-agnosticism across DDIM/Rex-RK4/IsoDiff, kNN vs. MLP lifting, embedding dimensionality sweeps, PCA/β-VAE baselines), which at least signals an attempt at thorough empirical characterization.
Reasonably detailed appendix on data acquisition/simulation pipelines (FEM fluid simulation, SimNIBS E-field modeling) could aid reproducibility for those specific simulated datasets.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the 'contrastive embedding' step is essentially an off-the-shelf application of CEBRA (Schneider et al., 2023) with a standard supervised InfoNCE loss, combined with standard spline/finite-difference/LSTM trajectory operators and a basic kNN decoder. The core technical contribution is largely an engineering pipeline stitching together existing components (DDIM/Rex-RK4 inversion, CEBRA, kNN regression, SciPy splines) rather than a new learning method, which is a thin basis for a research contribution.

The central interpolation experiments (Table 1, Fig. 2) appear methodologically circular: the spline/TEX curves are fit directly to the observed embedding sequence at the same points being 'interpolated,' so near-zero RMSE is close to tautological rather than evidence of a meaningfully 'dynamics-aligned' geometry. The comparison between Z-space and C-space is also confounded by dimensionality (very low-dimensional C trivially makes curve-fitting easier), so the claimed superiority of C over Z is not clearly attributable to contrastive structuring as opposed to simple dimensionality reduction.

The kNN lifting mechanism fundamentally limits the claimed capabilities of 'extrapolation' and 'counterfactual editing': since lifted latents are weighted combinations of nearby training latents, generated samples cannot be genuinely novel beyond the training latent manifold, which undercuts claims about true counterfactual generation (e.g., Fig. 3 responder/non-responder morphing) and long-range extrapolation. No analysis is given of how much edited samples differ from the nearest training examples.

The n-step-ahead prediction evaluation uses short held-out windows (7–12 frames) embedded within otherwise smooth, densely sampled sequences, which is a fairly weak test of genuine forecasting/extrapolation ability, and no comparison is made to dedicated forecasting baselines (neural ODEs, SSMs, or the cited physics-informed/video diffusion methods) despite those being extensively discussed in Related Work.

No statistical significance testing is reported despite overlapping confidence intervals/standard deviations in several tables (e.g., Table 1, Table 4), making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are robust.

Downstream utility is modest in at least one high-stakes application: the E-field responder/non-responder classifier only reaches F1=0.63, which is a weak basis for the clinical-targeting narrative implied by Fig. 3 and the paper's framing around personalized TMS treatment.

Presentation/quality issues suggest insufficient final-pass editing: the appendix contains a clearly leftover, malformed 'D REVISED RESULTS' table with broken LaTeX artifacts and truncated columns, which is unprofessional for a submission and raises concerns about the overall care taken in preparing the manuscript.

The general optimization framework in Eq. (2) is introduced but not concretely instantiated or ablated as a unified objective; the three 'editing operators' presented afterward are essentially independent heuristics (spline fitting, Taylor expansion, KDE-peak interpolation) rather than instances of a principled shared formalism, making the formal framing feel like unnecessary notation rather than a real contribution.

Ethical/data handling discussion is relatively generic given that two of five datasets involve clinical/patient data (TMS E-fields tied to HAMD-17 depression scores); there is little engagement with risks specific to using generative latent editing on sensitive psychiatric treatment-response data beyond a boilerplate impact statement.

strengths: Extensive empirical validation spanning five diverse spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, calcium imaging, TMS E-fields, facial expressions, and monkey motor cortex), which is unusually broad for a single paper and provides some evidence of generality.

Thorough ablation studies: comparison against PCA and beta-VAE baselines, kNN vs MLP lifting decoders, embedding dimensionality sweeps, and solver-agnosticism checks (DDIM vs Rex-RK4, cLDM vs IsoDiff), which strengthen the robustness claims.

The conceptual separation of 'editing' (in a compact contrastive space) from 'rendering' (in the full diffusion latent space) is intuitive and practically useful, addressing a real limitation of naive linear latent traversal in diffusion models.
Strong reproducibility effort: detailed appendices on data acquisition/simulation protocols, algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameters, and stated intent to release code and a new benchmark dataset.

Application to scientifically/clinically relevant problems (e.g., personalized TMS targeting, monkey motor cortex trajectories) gives the work potential translational significance beyond typical vision benchmarks.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination of existing components (CEBRA-based supervised InfoNCE embedding, kNN decoding, standard spline/Taylor/LSTM trajectory models) rather than a fundamentally new method; novelty lies mainly in the application/pipeline rather than in new algorithmic machinery.

Several reported results (e.g., RMSE of 0.00 for spline/TEX-2 in C-space in Table 1) appear suspiciously perfect and raise concerns about whether these are in-sample curve-fitting results rather than genuine held-out generalization; the paper does not clearly distinguish interpolation-on-training-trajectory from true generalization in all tables, which undermines confidence in the headline numbers.

No direct quantitative comparison against other relevant contrastive/disentanglement diffusion-editing baselines (e.g., NoiseCLR) on the same tasks/metrics, despite these being discussed at length in related work; comparisons are mostly against simple linear (Lerp/Slerp) or generic (PCA, beta-VAE) baselines rather than strong recent competitors.

The clinical neurostimulation application (responder vs. non-responder classification and KDE-based 'personalized targeting' trajectories) is based on weak classification performance (F1 ~0.63, imbalanced classes of 30 vs 80 patients) yet the paper frames this as suggesting 'a path to personalizing targeting strategies,' which risks overstating clinical significance without any validation against ground-truth treatment outcomes or expert review.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on pixel/latent-level metrics (PSNR, SSIM, RMSE); there is no perceptual/human evaluation or task-specific downstream validation (e.g., whether generated neural/E-field trajectories are physiologically plausible) to support interpretability and controllability claims beyond quantitative proxies.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, with some rough writing (e.g., grammatical issues in the introduction) and crowded, hard-to-read figures, which reduce accessibility and may obscure experimental details relevant to assessing soundness.

Limitations discussion is relatively generic (lossy embedding, local geometry, inversion cost) and does not engage with the more specific risks of overstated claims in the clinical use case or the possibility of leakage/overfitting in the near-perfect in-space trajectory fits.
